composites-001.question: Which correctly describes the main role of the matrix in a fiber-reinforced composite?
choices: It carries most of the load, and the role of the fibers is limited to preventing the matrix from cracking
It binds the fibers together to hold the shape, transfers load to the fibers through interfacial shear, and protects the fibers from abrasion and the environment
Its only role is to cancel the thermal expansion of the fibers, and it has no effect on mechanical properties
composites-001.explanation: In a fiber-reinforced composite, the strong, stiff fibers carry most of the load, while the matrix holds the fibers in their intended positions and orientations and gives the part its shape. External loads are transferred from the matrix to the fibers through shear at the fiber–matrix interface. The matrix also protects the fibers from damage, moisture and chemicals, and when one fiber breaks it keeps the crack from running straight into neighboring fibers. Saying the matrix carries most of the load reverses the roles of fiber and matrix. The matrix strongly influences the strength perpendicular to the fibers, the compressive strength and the interlaminar strength, so saying it has no effect on mechanical properties is also wrong.

composites-002.question: A composite of carbon fiber and epoxy has a carbon fiber mass fraction of 70%. Taking the density of carbon fiber as 1.80 g/cm³ and that of epoxy as 1.20 g/cm³, and assuming no voids, which value is closest to the fiber volume fraction?
choices: About 70%
About 78%
About 61%
composites-002.explanation: Volume is mass divided by density. In 100 g of composite, the fiber volume is 70/1.80 ≈ 38.9 cm³ and the resin volume is 30/1.20 = 25.0 cm³, so the fiber volume fraction is Vf = 38.9/(38.9 + 25.0) ≈ 0.61, about 61%. Because the fiber is denser than the resin, the volume fraction is smaller than the mass fraction. About 70% takes the mass fraction directly as the volume fraction; rule-of-mixtures calculations need the volume fraction. About 78% is the value calculated with the fiber and resin densities swapped. Real moldings may contain voids, so Vf and void content are checked by density measurement or the burn-off method.

composites-003.question: For a composite of aligned continuous fibers, which correctly describes when to use the isostrain and isostress forms of the rule of mixtures?
choices: Loading parallel to the fibers is approximated by the isostrain form and loading perpendicular to them by the isostress form; the former gives an upper bound on Young's modulus and the latter a lower bound
Loading parallel to the fibers is approximated by the isostress form and loading perpendicular to them by the isostrain form
The isostrain form holds in both directions, and Young's modulus does not depend on direction
composites-003.explanation: When loaded parallel to the fibers, fiber and matrix stretch by the same amount like springs connected in parallel, so the isostrain form E₁ = VfEf + VmEm applies. When loaded perpendicular to the fibers, fiber and matrix carry the same stress like springs in series, so the isostress form 1/E₂ = Vf/Ef + Vm/Em is used as an approximation. At the same volume fraction, the isostrain form gives an upper bound on Young's modulus and the isostress form a lower bound (the Voigt and Reuss bounds). The second choice swaps parallel and perpendicular. The modulus of unidirectional material differs greatly between the fiber and transverse directions, so saying it does not depend on direction is also wrong. The actual transverse modulus is often somewhat higher than the isostress form predicts, and corrections such as the Halpin–Tsai equations are used.

composites-004.question: A composite of glass fibers (Young's modulus 72 GPa) aligned in one direction at a volume fraction of 40% in a resin (Young's modulus 3.0 GPa) is loaded in tension parallel to the fibers. In the elastic range, which value is closest to the fraction of the load carried by the fibers?
choices: About 40%
About 94%
About 6%
composites-004.explanation: In tension parallel to the fibers, fiber and resin have equal strains, so the force each carries is proportional to the product of volume fraction and Young's modulus. The fiber share is VfEf/(VfEf + VmEm) = 0.40 × 72 / (0.40 × 72 + 0.60 × 3.0) = 28.8/30.6 ≈ 0.94, about 94%. About 40% assumes the load is proportional to the volume fraction and ignores the difference in modulus. About 6% is the share carried by the resin, mistaken for the fiber share. Even with less than half the volume as fiber, the fibers support almost all the load, so the strength and stiffness in the fiber direction are set almost entirely by the fiber properties.

composites-005.question: A composite contains glass fibers (Young's modulus 72 GPa) aligned in one direction at a volume fraction of 50% in a resin (Young's modulus 3.0 GPa). Using the isostress rule of mixtures, which value is closest to the Young's modulus perpendicular to the fibers?
choices: About 5.8 GPa
About 37.5 GPa
About 0.17 GPa
composites-005.explanation: Perpendicular to the fibers, fiber and resin are treated as lying in series and carrying the same stress, so 1/E₂ = Vf/Ef + Vm/Em is used. 1/E₂ = 0.50/72 + 0.50/3.0 = 0.00694 + 0.1667 = 0.1736 GPa⁻¹, so E₂ = 1/0.1736 ≈ 5.76 GPa, about 5.8 GPa. About 37.5 GPa is the modulus in the fiber direction from the isostrain form 0.50 × 72 + 0.50 × 3.0. About 0.17 GPa forgets to take the reciprocal. The transverse modulus stays close to that of the compliant resin, only about 15% (about 1/6.5) of the modulus in the fiber direction. This is why unidirectional material is not used in parts loaded perpendicular to the fibers.

composites-006.question: Which correctly compares carbon-fiber-reinforced plastic (CFRP) and glass-fiber-reinforced plastic (GFRP)?
choices: GFRP conducts electricity, so it readily causes galvanic corrosion when in contact with aluminum alloys
CFRP is transparent to radio waves and highly insulating, so it suits radar covers and electrical insulating parts
CFRP has a low density and high Young's modulus and so excels in specific stiffness, but it is expensive and, being conductive, readily causes corrosion in contact with aluminum alloys
composites-006.explanation: Carbon fiber has a density of about 1.8 g/cm³, lower than glass fiber (about 2.5 g/cm³), and a Young's modulus of about 230 GPa or more, over three times that of glass fiber (about 70 GPa), so CFRP excels in specific stiffness and specific strength and is used in aircraft and sporting goods. However, it is expensive, and because carbon fiber conducts electricity and has a noble electrode potential, contact with aluminum alloys readily causes galvanic corrosion of the aluminum; countermeasures include placing a layer of glass fiber between them. It is CFRP that conducts electricity, not GFRP. Transparency to radio waves and high insulation are characteristics of GFRP, which is used for radomes, electrical insulating parts, and inexpensive boat hulls and bathtubs.

composites-007.question: Which value is closest to the ratio CFRP/steel of the specific modulus (Young's modulus/density) in the fiber direction, for unidirectional CFRP (Young's modulus 140 GPa in the fiber direction, density 1.6 g/cm³) and steel (Young's modulus 210 GPa, density 7.9 g/cm³)?
choices: About 0.67
About 3.3
About 4.9
composites-007.explanation: The specific modulus is 140/1.6 = 87.5 for CFRP and 210/7.9 ≈ 26.6 for steel (both in GPa/(g/cm³)), so the ratio is 87.5/26.6 ≈ 3.3. CFRP has the lower Young's modulus itself, but its density is about one fifth, so at equal weight it is about 3.3 times as stiff. About 0.67 compares only the moduli (140/210), and about 4.9 looks only at the density ratio (7.9/1.6). Note that this value applies only in the fiber direction; perpendicular to the fibers, the specific modulus is far lower than that of steel. Real structures compensate for direction by laminating, so the specific-stiffness advantage is smaller than this value.

composites-008.question: When a short fiber embedded in a matrix is loaded in tension along its length, which correctly describes the distribution of tensile stress within the fiber? Assume the interface does not slip and transfers load at a constant shear stress.
choices: Nearly zero at both ends, increasing with distance from the ends through interfacial shear, and reaching a constant maximum in the middle if the fiber is long enough
Uniform along the whole length, independent of fiber length
Maximum at both ends and decreasing toward the middle
composites-008.explanation: Almost no load is transferred through the fiber end faces, so the fiber stress is nearly zero at the ends. Moving away from an end, load enters gradually through the interfacial shear stress τ, and the stress increases roughly in proportion to the distance from the end. If the fiber is long enough, beyond a certain distance the fiber and matrix strains match and the stress reaches a constant maximum. The length needed for this maximum to reach the fiber's tensile strength is the critical fiber length lc; the strength is reached at a distance lc/2 from the end. If the fiber is much longer than lc, the low-stress end portions make up a small fraction, and reinforcement close to that of continuous fibers is obtained. A stress uniform along the whole length is the idealization for continuous fibers, and saying the stress is maximum at the ends gets it backward.

composites-009.question: Which statement about the in-plane stiffness of a laminate in which unidirectional plies are stacked crosswise and symmetrically, as in [0/90]ₛ, is correct?
choices: The Young's moduli in the 0° and 90° directions are equal, and the 45° direction is the same too, so the laminate is isotropic in plane
Only the 0° direction has a high Young's modulus, and the 90° direction has the modulus of the resin alone
The Young's moduli in the 0° and 90° directions are nearly equal, but in the 45° direction no fibers take tension directly, so the low in-plane shear stiffness dominates and the modulus is small
composites-009.explanation: In [0/90]ₛ, loading in the 0° direction is carried along the fibers of the 0° plies and loading in the 90° direction along the fibers of the 90° plies, so the moduli in the two directions are nearly equal. Loaded at 45°, however, the fibers of every ply are 45° off the load direction, and the deformation becomes mainly in-plane shear supported by the resin, so the modulus drops considerably. To approach in-plane isotropy, ±45° plies are added to make a quasi-isotropic layup such as [0/±45/90]ₛ. Saying the 45° direction is the same overlooks this point. In the 90° direction the fibers of the 90° plies carry the load, so the modulus is not that of the resin alone. Note that in any layup the through-thickness direction is supported by the resin, so susceptibility to delamination remains.

composites-010.question: When glass fibers are used to reinforce a resin, what is the main purpose of treating the fiber surface with a silane coupling agent?
choices: To smooth the fiber surface and reduce friction with the resin
To strengthen interfacial adhesion with molecules that bond to both the inorganic fiber surface and the organic resin, improving load transfer and water resistance
To lower the thermal conductivity of the fibers and slow the resin cure during molding
composites-010.explanation: A silane coupling agent is a molecule with an alkoxysilyl group at one end that bonds to the hydroxyl groups on the glass surface, and at the other end a group such as amino, epoxy or vinyl that reacts with the resin. Because it links the inorganic glass and the organic resin by chemical bonds, interfacial adhesion is strengthened and load is transferred more readily to the fibers through interfacial shear. It is also very effective at preventing water from penetrating the interface and weakening adhesion, limiting the loss of strength in humid environments. Smoothing the surface to reduce friction would weaken load transfer, the opposite of the purpose. Changing the thermal conductivity or the cure rate of the resin is not the purpose of a coupling agent.

composites-011.question: Which correctly describes the properties of a metal matrix composite (MMC) of an aluminum alloy reinforced with SiC particles?
choices: Compared with the aluminum alloy matrix, its Young's modulus and wear resistance are higher and its coefficient of thermal expansion is lower, but its ductility and toughness are lower
Compared with the aluminum alloy matrix, its coefficient of thermal expansion is higher and its ductility is greatly improved
SiC particles do not react with molten aluminum at all, so no reaction products form at the interface whatever the processing temperature
composites-011.explanation: Adding SiC particles, which have a high Young's modulus of about 400 GPa and a low coefficient of thermal expansion of about 4×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹, makes the Young's modulus and wear resistance of the composite higher than those of the aluminum alloy matrix and its thermal expansion coefficient lower. Because the thermal expansion can be brought close to that of semiconductors and ceramic substrates, these composites are used for heat spreaders for power semiconductors and similar parts. On the other hand, cracks form easily around the hard particles, so ductility and toughness decrease. The statement that thermal expansion increases and ductility improves is backward on both counts. Also, SiC can react with hot molten aluminum to form brittle Al₄C₃, and the reaction is suppressed by controlling the processing temperature and the Si content of the matrix.

composites-012.question: In a ceramic matrix composite (CMC) reinforced with SiC fibers, what is the main purpose of applying a thin coating of boron nitride (BN) or pyrolytic carbon at the fiber–matrix interface?
choices: To bond the interface as strongly as possible so that cracks run straight through the fibers
To lower the melting point of the ceramic matrix so it can be sintered at a lower temperature
To make the interface suitably weak so that cracks are deflected along it and energy is absorbed by fiber debonding and pull-out
composites-012.explanation: The ceramic matrix is brittle, so under load cracks first form in the matrix. If the interface is too strong, these cracks run straight through the fibers and the material fractures all at once, just like a monolithic ceramic. A layered, easily sliding coating such as BN or pyrolytic carbon makes the interface suitably weak, so cracks are deflected along the interface, and the fibers bridge the crack while absorbing considerable energy through debonding and pull-out. The result is a fracture mode that does not fail suddenly, with a large increase in apparent toughness. Bonding the interface as strongly as possible is the approach for improving load transfer in resin matrices, and it is counterproductive in CMCs. The coating is not meant to lower the sintering temperature.
